<reason>Both sides delivered an exceptionally sharp, well-grounded exchange, but Side B won by dismantling Side A's mechanism for mitigating short-term displacement. Side A argued strongly that scarcity causes uncompensated displacement via rent hikes and that by-right density can be paired with codified interim relocation and replacement-housing mandates cross-subsidized by added market-rate units. However, Side B methodically exposed the practical flaws in that mechanism: promising "comparable interim housing nearby" during three years of construction contradicts the premise that the neighborhood faces an acute vacancy shortage, and attaching a massive per-tenant replacement liability to newly upzoned land creates a perverse incentive for speculators to use cash buyouts or constructive evictions to empty older walk-ups before pulling permits. Furthermore, when Side A argued that developers would simply leave older rentals alone if replacement mandates were too costly and build on parking lots and commercial sites instead, Side B effectively turned that admission to show that municipalities should directly target density to non-residential and affluent parcels rather than painting a speculative demolition target on existing low-rent apartments.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [B4.3]-[B4.4], Side B turned Side A's own answers to the pressure questions against its case: Side B showed that requiring "comparable interim housing nearby" contradicts Side A's premise of a local vacancy shortage, that Side A's admission that some tenants will take "a payout elsewhere" exposes how upzoning incentivizes pre-permit buyouts to erase replacement liabilities, and that Side A's fallback—that developers will skip unprofitable teardowns and build on parking lots and commercial sites—concedes that older rentals should have been protected from blanket by-right teardown entitlements in the first place.</best_rebuttal>
